definition: The button a pilot or controller holds down to transmit. While it is held, their own receiver is muted; when it is released, they can listen again.
Radio where everyone shares one frequency and only one person can transmit at a time, like a walkie-talkie. Aviation voice radio works this way.
A gate in the receiver that keeps the loudspeaker silent until a signal stronger than a set threshold arrives, so you do not have to listen to hiss.
The loud whistle heard when two transmitters on almost the same frequency are on the air together: their carriers beat against each other.
Two stations transmitting on the same frequency at the same moment. Listeners hear a squeal and neither message gets through. Also called being "stepped on".
An emergency frequency that many aircraft and ATC units listen to all the time: 121.5 MHz for civil aviation, 243.0 MHz for military aircraft.
How far apart neighbouring radio channels are. Aviation VHF uses 25 kHz, or 8.33 kHz where more channels are needed: three channels fit where one used to be.
Voice communication control system: the equipment that connects each controller's headset and keys to the right radios and telephone lines.
A transmit button that stays pressed, for example jammed or sat on. The radio keeps transmitting and blocks the frequency for everyone in range.
A strong transmitter on the next channel leaking into your receiver, because no filter can cut off a neighbouring frequency completely.
Radio sites keep a spare transmitter ready. If the main one fails, the controller or the system changes over to the standby so that voice keeps going out.
A place with antennas, transmitters and receivers, often on a hill and far from the control centre, connected to the controllers by lines.
Decibels compared with one milliwatt. 0 dBm is 1 mW, −30 dBm is a thousandth of that; a received radio signal is often around −60 to −100 dBm.
